messages.author: 1eec5310e38e5422
messages.subject: problem with construction of latent variable
parts:
Hello,

I am rather new to lavaan, so apologies if this has been asked before, but I am not sure how to find the answer.

As a first step in constructing my model I am trying to build a latent variable named dispersal potential, constructed of three measured variables: seed's falling velocity, seed's pappus width, and seed's mass. 
The natural relationship between this three variables is the following: falling velocity is positively correlated to pappus width and negatively to seed mass; seed mass and pappus width are positively correlated.


When I try to use the following latent variable:
DP =~ TV + Width + Mass

I get the following errors:
lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!
** WARNING ** Estimates below are most likely unreliable

and the estimate of the latent variable looks like this:



What is the proper way to construct this latent variable?

Thank you in advance,

Efrat

If, for example, I want to model the following: DP is constructed from Pappus_width Seed_mass and Falling_velocity, and it is affected by Veg_height, Veg_cover and Rosette. 
I understand the first line should be:
DP <- Pappus_width + Seed_mass + Falling_velocity

But should I model the affecting variables with a regression or a latent variable? So, should DP be:
DP =~ Veg_height + Veg_cover + Rosette
or should it be:
DP ~ Veg_height + Veg_cover + Rosette
?

Thanks in advance,
Efrat

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: problem with construction of latent variable
parts:
Efrat,
  I am developing mixed feelings about being able to recommend SEMNET as a source of fact-based advice.  So, I will try of offer a brief answer that stays fairly focused on lavaan syntax and is hopefully not inappropriate to the lavaan help forum.

  First let me offer a correction to your first example.  The formative syntax is <~, not <-.  The former sticks with the tilde themed operators in lavaan model syntax.  The latter is used in general R as an assignment operator and thus avoided in model syntax.

  Here are two canonical references that offer a good place to enter the literature.

Bollen, K. A. & Lenox, R. (1991). Conventional wisdom on measurement: A structural equation perspective. Psychological Bulletin, 110, 305-314. doi: 10.1037/0033-2909.110.2.305

Edwards, J. R. & Bagozzi, R. P. (2000). On the nature and direction of relationships between constructs and measures. Psychological Methods, 5, 155-174. doi: 10.1037/1082-989X.5.2.155

  The formative measure syntax using <~ is just a convenience.  It is a good exercise to specify a formative model with and without using this syntax just to confirm to yourself that you understand what it does and to see that you can obtain identical results either way.  You can create a latent variable in lavaan syntax with LV =~ 0.

  In the statistical model, there is no difference between a loading parameter and an effect coefficient.  To see this, consider that the LISREL model requires parameterizing path model effects as effects between dummy latent variables.  Moving a parameter between matrices does not have any statistical impact.

  Reflective measurement models are just common causes and formative models are just common effects (although identification requires that such latent variables also be common causes of outcome variables).  These labels do not affect the underlying statistical model.  The main thing to avoid here is to allow yourself to get sucked into the language of scale development if you really have no intention to develop a re-usable scale that serves a purpose outside this one data analytic effort.  You do not want to set yourself up for reviewers to burst your bubble by questioning exaggerated claims of measurement.

Markus, K. A. (2018).  Three conceptual impediments to developing scale theory for formative scales.  Methodology, 14, 156-164.  doi: 10.1027/1614-2241/a000154

  Turning to your final two examples, the first treats DP as a common cause of the other variables.  The second treats DP as a common effect.  Within the context of the larger model, the first option treats DP as the sole mediator of all effects from the first three variables to the last three.  That implication is commendably testable but you need to judge whether it is scientifically plausible.  The second example makes a gratuitous distinction between the first three and last three variables because they are all causes of DP.  This second model could equally well be specified as a formative model with six items or as a regression with six predictors.

  This second model is not identified without some effects of DP in the model.  Otherwise, there is nothing to pin down what outcome of the six observed variables DP should represent.  In the end, formative latent variables are just common factors of their outcomes.

  I hope that that was helpful and not too far off topic.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: problem with construction of latent variable
parts:
Efrat--
 Efrat--

     I think your answer will involve nonparametric causal inference methods. It sounds like there are multiplicative relations at work, and also sounds like you are highly uncertain about the functional form of your model. Nonparametric methods do not attempt to estimate model parameters (because you need a functional form to do that) but focus on quantifying the overall impact of one variable on another. I am attaching a paper that will give you an introduction.

     A large part of the attraction of the factor model lies in the claim that this approach “accounts for measurement error,” while other methods do not. I’m not going to explore that argument, but it does require that the factor model is correctly specified. There may be questions about the impact of “measurement error” on your results, including the likelihood that such errors create an endogeneity problem with your results.

--Ed Rigdon
